issues.legal_issue: The power of judicial superintendence cannot be used to reappraise evidence and overturn reasonably possible concurrent findings of fact made by subordinate courts.
material_facts: In an eviction suit, the trial court found that the landlord had not established a bona fide and reasonable requirement and that greater hardship would be caused to the tenant by eviction.
The appellate court affirmed those findings after considering the evidence.
The High Court, acting in supervisory jurisdiction, reassessed the evidence and reached different conclusions on the landlord’s requirement and comparative hardship.
The Supreme Court found the lower courts’ conclusions to be a reasonably possible appreciation of the evidence, with nothing perverse or so grossly unjust as to require supervisory intervention.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by interfering with the concurrent findings of fact. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the decisions of the trial court and appellate court were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers judicial superintendence, to be exercised sparingly to keep subordinate courts within the bounds of their authority, not to correct mere errors or act as a court of appeal on facts. Even an apparent error of fact is not a basis for appellate reappraisal under Article 227. The Court relied on Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, Assam, and Bathutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarta; Waryam Singh also referred to Dalmia Jain Airways Ltd. v. Sukumar Mukherjee.

rule.if: supervisory_review_of_eviction_case and concurrent_fact_findings and findings_reasonably_possible and not exceptional_gross_injustice

predicates.supervisory_review_of_eviction_case: The matter is a supervisory review of a decision in an eviction case.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The subordinate trial and appellate courts reached the same factual conclusions after considering the evidence.
predicates.findings_reasonably_possible: The evidence and circumstances reasonably support the factual conclusions reached by the subordinate courts.
predicates.exceptional_gross_injustice: The findings are so grossly wrong, unjust, or shocking that intervention is necessary in the interest of justice.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns an eviction case, the subordinate courts made concurrent findings that are reasonably supported by the evidence, and no exceptional gross injustice is present, supervisory interference with those findings is unjustified.
